question: The increase in the cost of fertilisers and other agricultural inputs is putting serious pressure on the competitiveness and viability of European farms. In May 2026, the Commission presented an action plan to strengthen the availability and affordability of fertilisers, providing for financial support among other things. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What level of funding, in its view, could be directed to Greece and through which financial tools?
When are the relevant measures expected to be in place and what criteria will be used to distribute the funding among the Member States?
Has it specifically assessed the evolution of the cost of fertiliser and other agricultural inputs in Greece, in relation to income and farm-gate prices?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.10.2026) On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted a Fertiliser Action Plan1 which includes shortterm and long-term measures to boost domestic production and provide targeted support to farmers, while remaining aligned with the EU’s climate and environmental objectives.

In this context, on 27 July 2026 the Commission adopted a EUR 540 million exceptional support for farmers facing high input costs2, out of which Greece received almost EUR 20.8 million. Member States can complement this aid up to 200% with national funds.

On 13 July 2026, targeted measures enabling Member States to maximise support available under the current Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans for farmers facing rising input costs, including through liquidity support, more flexible advanced payments and adjustments of 2027 direct payments, were also adopted3.

Moreover, under the Middle East Crisis Temporary State Aid Framework adopted by the Commission on 29 April 20264, the Commission approved a Greek State aid scheme to mitigate the impact of higher fertiliser costs for farmers, amounting to EUR 41 million on 16 July 20265.

The Commission regularly monitors agricultural input prices, including fertilisers, and agricultural output prices across Member States, based on Eurostat data. This allows for assessing input costs and output prices in individual Member States as compared to the EU average.

The Commission didn’t carry out a specific assessment of fertiliser and other agricultural input costs in Greece in relation to farm income and farm-gate prices. As in many Member States, there is no publicly available benchmark for fertiliser prices paid by farmers. Through the Fertiliser Action Plan, the Commission aims to enhance market transparency and improve the availability of market information.
